The other day I walked outside my apartment in New York and noticed the slightest hint of a chill in the morning air. And I could only think of one thing: the postseason is almost here. The long baseball season is drawing to a close. The delight of October awaits.
And then …
Oh, yeah. The lockout.
The next few months could reshape the future of baseball. I suppose we shall see how it goes. Until then, let’s take some questions. As always, they have been edited for clarity.
Advertisement
Which wild-card team has the best chance to upset a division winner? — bbrathizza2075
There are a lot of worthy candidates, especially in the National League. But I would have to say the Yankees, if only because on paper, the Yankees should be the best team in the American League, even if they are unlikely to catch the American League East. The Yankees lead the AL in run differential by a significant margin. No AL lineup has hit more home runs. In Cam Schlittler, they employ the Cy Young favorite. And they still have Aaron Judge.
So the Yankees would be my pick, but the talent on the other wild-card clubs is immense. The Phillies can line up Cristopher Sánchez, Zack Wheeler and, if he’s healthy, Jesús Luzardo in a five-game series. Good luck. Pete Crow-Armstrong has been the best player in baseball for a Cubs team that boasts the best offense in baseball. A healthy Nick Pivetta provides San Diego with enough rotation stability for a short series, in which their bullpen would be hellish to face. And the Padres, who would likely face the Dodgers, have shown a willingness in recent years to stand and trade blows with baseball’s reigning champs.
And, really, what qualifies as an upset? If the 98-win Rays lose to the 94-win Yankees in a five-game series, would it really be shocking? Same story with the Phillies or the Cubs facing the Brewers. These teams will be quite evenly matched. It should be an entertaining October.
Which National League fanbase would be MOST disappointed if its team doesn’t hoist the commissioner’s trophy in 2026? Big narrative-ball postseason for Brewers, Phillies and even Cubs fans in my opinion. — Jacob N.
I think it’s a toss-up between Milwaukee and Philadelphia. And I would lean toward the Phillies.
When it comes to the Brewers, a lot of folks in baseball have asked the question: If not now, when? Well, the team made clear, in part by declining to go bonkers and acquire Tarik Skubal, that it rejects the premise. And the Brewers brain trust may be wise to do so. This team is well-situated to contend in 2026, but also well beyond 2026. Jackson Chourio is 22. Jacob Misiorowski is 24. Logan Henderson is 24. Brice Turang is practically ancient at 26. Jesús Made and Luis Peña are on the way. This team isn’t going anywhere.
Right. Right?
Well …
Baltimore fans felt the same way after a 101-win campaign in 2023. Instead, they’ve watched the Orioles degrade from budding juggernaut into a last-place club. And while I do not foresee that fate for the Brewers, it remains within the realm of possibility. Misiorowski may not stay healthy beyond this season. The 2026 campaign could be this group’s best chance to win the first championship in franchise history.
Advertisement
Even so, I don’t think the psychological blow of an early exit would sting Brewers fans like it would Phillies fans. There is just so much frustration stored up within that fanbase, dating to that shocking collapse in the 2023 National League Championship Series. There are also legitimate questions about how long the window will remain open for this group. Again, it comes back to age. Kyle Schwarber is 33. Bryce Harper turns 34 in October. Zack Wheeler is 36. Trea Turner is playing below-replacement-level at 33 — and his contract will not expire until 2033. The farm system has not produced much in recent years, and Dave Dombrowski has not done well on the free-agent market.
So while Brewers fans may be infuriated about the unfairness of MLB’s system, and while they may lament another missed opportunity, they can credibly believe they will have another shot in 2027. That is harder to fathom for Phillies fans.
The first two teams to clinch playoff berths were the Rays and Brewers. Could you shed any light on the Tampa Bay model both teams adhere to? — Gary D.
Back in 2021, I wrote a lengthy feature about the Rays and their ruthless roster building. The simplest way to describe it is they make a lot of transactions, and that churning allows them to occasionally unearth stars.
Here is one example. Back in 2008, the Rays chose Tim Beckham with the first overall pick in the draft. Beckham was essentially a bust. He took five years to reach the majors and never really hit. In 2017, after nearly a decade of trying to develop him, Tampa Bay dealt Beckham to Baltimore for minor-league pitcher Tobias Myers. He spent a few seasons in Tampa Bay’s farm system before getting traded to Cleveland for a teenage prospect from the Dominican Republic. You may have heard of him by now: Junior Caminero. And Caminero has become the sort of star the Rays once envisioned Beckham could have been. The team turned a failure into a smashing success.
Now, most front offices don’t get a decade to oversee decisions like this. Andrew Friedman was in charge when Beckham was drafted. Chaim Bloom was running the show when Beckham was traded. And Erik Neander, who has worked in the organization since 2007, was the head of baseball operations for the Caminero deal. But the organizational ethos hasn’t changed all that much over the past decade.
Advertisement
Milwaukee also tends toward roster churn but is a tad less aggressive than Tampa Bay. The Brewers are run by Rays alum Matt Arnold, and that man does love a three-team trade. They can find great production on the margins, as they have this season with Jake Bauers. And they are unafraid to deal star players as their contracts expire, as they did in recent years with Corbin Burnes, Devin Williams and Freddy Peralta. Where Milwaukee really excels is scouting Latin America. It signed Chourio and outfielder Luis Lara out of Venezuela. They signed Made and Peña out of the Dominican.
These are the things that small-market teams would like to emulate. Do well in the draft. Don’t stay static on the margins of the roster. And excel in finding stars out of the international market. If it was easy, every team would do it.
Do you think we have seen the last of Shohei Ohtani as a pitcher/starter? — Tae K.
I do not. He will pitch again. But how the Dodgers deploy him will be fascinating.
Multiple things can be true:
1. Shohei Ohtani might be the best pitcher in the world.
He demonstrated that during his 14 starts this season. He posted a 1.79 ERA while striking out 10 batters per nine innings. And he did that while toting the responsibility of batting leadoff as the designated hitter most days in between outings. He looked, in a word, awesome.
2. As he enters his mid-30s, Ohtani probably cannot complete a full season as a two-way player.
The basic story of Ohtani’s professional life is people within baseball telling him, “Hey! You can’t do that,” and Ohtani responding, “Well, actually, I can.” But Father Time is undefeated, and Ohtani has learned that the two-way load is far tougher to shoulder at 32 than it was at 27. He is currently on the injured list dealing with problems with his neck, knee and biceps. And there may be other maladies the famously private Ohtani has not revealed. Suffice to say, he is quite banged up, and no one within the Dodgers organization is thrilled about the situation.
Advertisement
These two facts — Ohtani’s greatness and his fallibility — present the Dodgers with a conflict. There is a clear compromise: the team should ask him to spend the first half of the season as a hitter and then use the second half to build up arm strength so he can be available to pitch in October. Problem solved!
Well, not exactly. Ohtani has agency in this situation. He may not want to give up the full-season two-way dream so easily. He may still want to prove that he can do in his 30s what he did in his 20s. He may still want to say, “Well, actually, I can.” And the Dodgers may not want to scuffle with the face of the franchise. It will be a delicate dance.
How Ohtani feels about his future is unclear. He has not spoken to reporters since Sept. 7, and did not accompany the club on its current trip to Miami and Cincinnati. But he has been staunch his entire career about wanting to remain a two-way player. “The reason why I’m a two-way player is because that’s who I am,” he said during the 2025 postseason. “And it’s what I can do.”
I still think he can be a two-way player, and I would be shocked if he tried to only hit moving forward. But the prospect of him being a healthy two-way player over the course of a 162-game season feels more like a fantasy than a reality. Then again, Ohtani has shown us, over and over in his career, that he can make dreams come true.
Catchers were the overwhelming best at ABS challenges, but I am curious how they fared at challenging as batters compared to batters at other positions. — Anonymous
Interesting premise.
I looked this up and found essentially no correlation. Now, there may be a connection, because while I am not a math wizard, I don’t think one unfinished season provides enough data for a sufficient sample size. At least this year, there is little evidence that, as hitters, catchers perform better than other hitters with ABS.
Dillon Dingler entered Monday’s games rated as the best challenger among catchers, according to FanGraphs. But as a hitter? Dingler graded below average. Same story for Hunter Goodman and J.T. Realmuto, the two catchers rated best behind Dingler.
Among the hitters, there were two catchers rated in Savant’s top 10 for ABS efficiency: Tyler Stephenson and Gabriel Moreno. Iván Herrera came in at No. 14. But then no catcher appears on the leaderboard until Brandon Valenzuela at No. 34. So, like I said, interesting premise, but no real correlation that this knucklehead who flunked geometry in high school can find.
Advertisement
For the last couple of decades, Major League Baseball has seemed to have a major “household name” gap with the NBA and NFL, and Rob Manfred once addressed this by complaining that Mike Trout wasn’t doing more to make himself famous. How is the league working to grow its fanbase and promote its product? — Alex R.
The owners are planning to lock out the players when the collective bargaining agreement expires on Dec. 1.
What are your most realistic thoughts on the lockout? — pollrobb
When I talk to people in baseball about the lockout, they usually say some version of the same thing: they really don’t know what will happen, but they think it will be bad. The negotiations will be contentious. The rhetoric will be vicious. They may well miss games.
My guess — and I will repeat that this is a guess — is that the lockout resolves at some point in March, with enough time to cram a 162-game season into the calendar, in a result similar to the last lockout. I do not foresee the players caving and accepting a salary cap. But it is also hard to identify, in that scenario, what would trigger the owners to stop pushing for one. Genuinely, I do not know how it will go, and anyone who tells you they do is probably overselling their insight.
Why would the players and league not work on solving 100 small things in negotiation now and figure out the big topic at the end? Is it really going to wreck what they have while fighting over billions of dollars? I truly enjoy the game and can’t believe they say it can all wait until December, so they can blame each other. Why not now? — Lynn Z.
To be fair, the two sides have traded a variety of proposals on issues besides the salary cap. They are negotiating. But the small stuff is small for a reason. And the big thing — the potential implementation of a salary cap — is much bigger than anything on the table in the previous round of negotiations. For the owners, the possibility of a cap means billions of dollars gained in franchise values. But for the players, accepting a cap means the collapse of the free-market system that the union has fought so strenuously to maintain for decades. These are existential questions for both sides. And neither side will be inclined to budge until the calendar flips into 2027 and spring training draws closer. So, buckle up. It is going to be a long, bumpy ride.

The Dodgers’ winning ways in September were briefly interrupted for two games against the Miami Marlins, but they have picked back up against the Cincinnati Reds, taking the first two games of a four-game set.
After Tarik Skubal shut down Cincinnati over seven innings on Monday, Yoshinobu Yamamoto continued the trend of marvelous results from the rotation with a seven-inning scoreless gem on Tuesday, working through a pair of lead-off walks while allowing just one hit while striking out seven. Yamamoto has amazed in his two most recent starts— both against the Reds— allowing just one run over 14 innings while racking up 17 strikeouts compared to just three walks.
Yamamoto held the Reds to just a 1-21 clip after walking his first two hitters of the game on Tuesday, and the right-hander managed to take a page out of Skubal’s playbook for his dominating efforts, notes Sonja Chen of MLB.com.
Yamamoto was able to learn from how the Reds approached Skubal the night before, and Snell was no doubt gathering similar information on Tuesday.
“That kind of encouraged me to be aggressive and attack the hitters,” Yamamoto said through interpreter Yoshihiro Sonoda.
The pitching has managed to hold their end of the bargain against Cincinnati this week, and Blake Snell looks to keep that trajectory in motion. On the offensive side of the ball, Teoscar Hernández has fortified the offense at Great American Ball Park, as the right-hander has crushed a pair of two-run home runs that put both games out of reach.
Hernández has once again found his stride that fans saw during spring training this year, and the Dodger outfielder’s recent success is the brainchild of hitting coach Aaron Bates, allowing Hernández to have a “twister tap” in his stride to the ball, per Maddie Lee of the Los Angeles Times.
“It was a great meeting we had,” Bates said. “We all talked about it, and then he felt comfortable enough to do it, and then the rest is to his credit. He’s just been who he is.”
“When Teo’s hips are loose that way, and his front leg looks like an Elvis knee, it’s a good sign for us,” Bates said. “Because that means that he can open and close it without his upper body going with it.”
Update on Shohei Ohtani
It’s an unusual feeling watching the Dodgers without Shohei Ohtani in the everyday lineup. So far, rookie Josue De Paula has filled in at DH to a small degree of success in limited time (.143/.368/.429, 19 PA) while the reigning two-time NL MVP recovers from multiple nagging issues.
Jack Harris of the California Post notes that Ohtani was able to take batting practice on Monday, and the team is optimistic that he can potentially return from the injured list before the end of the regular season.
“Today was positive,” Roberts said, “and hopefully we can just keep building towards that.”

CINCINNATI — Before each start, Yoshinobu Yamamoto does something remarkable.
Many pitchers long toss as part of their pregame routine. It's common practice at the high school level and above to warm up the arm, boot up the body, rev up the engine. Throwing a ball far is mighty similar, biomechanically, to throwing a ball fast.
But Yamamoto takes things to another level. After subjecting his muscles and ligaments to an elaborate stretching program, the Dodgers righty begins playing catch, gradually working his way toward the outer reaches of a big-league park's center-field grasslands. First 200 feet, then 250, 275, up to around 300. But instead of winding himself up with a few hop-steps like most long-tossers do, Yamamoto lets it fly from the relative standstill of his usual in-game windup.
It's a mesmerizing thing to witness — this 5-foot-10, 176-pound speck of cerulean catapulting a baseball 100 yards without the help of any real momentum. For a few seconds after release, Yamamoto stands frozen, balancing on his left leg with his right leg dangling in the air. The whole thing looks fake, like a lazy AI generation. How could a dude that small throw a ball that far that easily?
Such is the magic of Yamamoto: balance, intention, mechanical precision.
All those qualities and more were on display Tuesday in Cincinnati as the undersized hurler tore the Reds asunder. He worked seven scoreless innings, struck out seven and allowed just one hit.
After walking the first two hitters of the game, Yamamoto settled in. Following Elly De La Cruz's double in the third, the Dodgers starter retired the final 13 hitters he faced.
"He's able to reset on the fly. He's able to bear down and make pitches when he needs to," manager Dave Roberts explained after L.A.'s 4-0 win.
Yamamoto needed that adjustability Tuesday after an uncharacteristically poor start to the outing. He walked Cincinnati leadoff man Carlos Jorge, making just the fifth start of his MLB career, on four wayward offerings. It was the first time in Yamamoto's stateside tenure that he walked the first batter of the game on four pitches. He was similarly over-careful with the following hitter, walking De La Cruz on a 3-1 count. Jorge reached third base on a sac fly but got no further, as Yamamoto escaped the frame with no damage.
"At the beginning, because I [didn't] have my usual stuff mechanically, so mentally I was very calm, and then still kept composed, so I was able to make an adjustment on time," Yamamoto said afterward.
From there, it was business as usual, with Yamamoto deploying his typical barrage of splitters, curves and heaters. It was metronomical, almost humdrum, the way Yamamoto eased through the outing with little trouble. You blinked, and he was in the seventh with a zero on the board.
His entire season has carried a similar energy. The National League's overabundance of headline hurlers has been one of this campaign's main storylines. Jacob Misiorowski looks primed to win his first Cy Young behind a historic, bat-missing stat line. Chris Sale, Cristopher Sánchez, Jesús Luzardo and Chase Burns have all been excellent as well. Those characters, to a certain extent, have overshadowed Yamamoto's contributions.
This tumultuous Dodgers season, too, has stolen some of the shine. So much attention has been paid to the health and exploits of Shohei Ohtani and his quest to reestablish himself as a two-way dynamo over a full season. L.A.'s acquisition of Tarik Skubal overtook the trade deadline. Through it all, Yamamoto has remained magnificently consistent.
And with October just around the corner, the 2025 World Series hero is looking primed to carry the torch for the Dodgers once again.

Los Angeles Dodgers newest star pitcher Tarik Skubal reveals the impact of Will Smith calling his pitches.
Smith has come back from his neck injury and made an immediate impression on the pitching staff.
Skubal, who joined the team at the trade deadline, hasn’t been able to work much with Smith since Smith’s injury.
However, since coming back to the Dodgers on September 1st, Smith has caught three games for Skubal and left the two-time Cy Young winner quite impressed.
In those three starts, he has a 1.80 ERA over 20 innings with four walks and 20 strikeouts.
Most notably, in his last start, Skubal went seven innings, allowing no runs, one walk, and nine strikeouts in what became the best start of his Dodgers career.
After the game, Skubal told reporters that Smith called every pitch, never shaking him off once during the outing.
“Yeah, I think it’s just kind of reading, reacting to what situations, or reading swings,” Skubal said.
“And honestly, a lot of that’s Will. Like, I trust him with calling every pitch. I think I shook one time tonight, so we’re in pretty good rhythm.”
How Smith is helping Skubal settle in with the Dodgers
Skubal has said he’s been thinking too much about pitch selection rather than focusing on execution, leading to inconsistent results.
Since joining the Dodgers, Skubal has felt he underestimated how much familiarity with the catchers and other members of the pitching staff matters.
Now, he is working hard to focus on that line of communication.
“I think just trying to get on the same page with everybody here, you know, catching department, pitching department, constantly learning each other and developing those relationships,” Skubal explained.
“And I probably underestimated that a little bit, but just communicating, having open dialogue with all these guys on what I like to do, what I’m comfortable with.
“And then, honestly, some things I’m uncomfortable with, working on those things because it’s gonna be important.
“I think we’re developing a really good relationship and rhythm, just with me and everybody else, the catchers and the pitching department.”
With Skubal settling in and starting to make the most out of a pitching operation that has succeeded over the last several years, this bodes very well for the postseason outlook.

CINCINNATI — The Dodgers can only hope it looks this good in October.
One night after Tarik Skubal went seven innings in his first scoreless outing as a Dodger, Yoshinobu Yamamoto matched him, allowing only one hit in his seven scoreless innings as the Dodgers shut out the Cincinnati Reds, 4-0, on Tuesday night.
“When you’re writing in the lineup and you see those guys, and one trying to up the other guy, and then now you got Snell going tomorrow – you feel good about preventing runs,” Dodgers manager Dave Roberts said.
“A team like the Reds right now, where they’re scuffling a little bit, it’s daunting when you see a starter like those guys that we’re running out there.”
The win moved the Dodgers (92-59) within one day of clinching their 13th NL West division title in the past 14 seasons. Their magic number is one after the second-place San Diego Padres (82-69) lost to the Colorado Rockies later Tuesday night.
The Dodgers’ lead over the Atlanta Braves (89-63) for the No. 2 seed in the National League remains 3½ games. Their magic number to clinch a first-round bye is eight.
All of that makes the final two weeks of the regular season a chance for the Dodgers to get things right for October and their three-peat pursuit. The starting rotation appears to be there already.
Skubal has a 1.73 ERA over his past four starts. With Tuesday’s outing, Yamamoto’s ERA is 1.79 over his past seven starts. Blake Snell starts on Wednesday – and he has given up a total of only four runs in six starts since returning from elbow surgery. Only fourth starter Tyler Glasnow (eight runs in 10 innings over his past two starts) seems to have some work to do before being October-ready.
“Yeah, pretty good,” first baseman Freddie Freeman said after his first three-hit game since Aug. 17. “You have Blake Snell going tomorrow. Tyler on the back end of that too. Roki’s on his way back.
“It’s a special pitching staff. It really is. So as an offense, we just need to score a few runs for them, just like we did last year.”
Yamamoto started Tuesday by giving the Reds hope – he walked the first two batters he faced – then he took it away, retiring 21 of the next 22 batters he faced.
“They took a little moment for me,” Yamamoto said through his interpreter of the mound visit from catcher Hunter Feduccia and pitching coach Mark Prior that followed the walks. “They came up to me and, ‘Hey, how you doing?’ and just checked in on me. And then I was able to get back to my normal rhythm.”
Elly De La Cruz had the only hit off Yamamoto, a double into the left-field corner with two outs in the third inning.
But even that was a victory – Yamamoto kept him in the ballpark after De La Cruz had hit a home run in each of the previous four games between the Dodgers and Reds. He then retired the next 13 batters in order, getting six of his seven strikeouts.
“After the first two hitters, it was vintage Yama,” Roberts said. “Just attacking, not trying to be too fine. Not giving these guys too much credit. And yeah, at first, it didn’t look promising as far as pitch count, the two walks. But then he kind of dialed things in, like he’s been known to do.”
The Dodgers gave him a lead in the second inning when Max Muncy was hit by a pitch and Tommy Edman and Hunter Feduccia followed with singles. They added to it in the third inning with a two-run home run from Teoscar Hernandez, who remains hot – 24 for 63 (.381) in his past 18 games.
“It’s been very helpful,” Roberts said of Hernandez’s late-season renaissance. “As certain guys are not seeing the ball as well, it’s nice to kind of backfill with guys like Teo swinging the bat. And when you can slug like he can, you can win baseball games, and he can carry us for a while. The last 10 days, something like that, it’s been really good from him. The defense ticked up. The at-bat quality, the taking walks, all of it. I can’t say enough about what he’s done the last 10 days.”
De La Cruz had another hit, a single in the ninth inning that put runners on the corners for the Reds with no outs. Tanner Scott struck out Sal Stewart, Jose Trevino and Eugenio Suarez to close out the shutout.

CINCINNATI –– There’s not much the Dodgers can do, manager Dave Roberts said Tuesday afternoon, to get their all-important rotation ready for the added workload that will come in the postseason.
Over the final couple weeks of the regular season, they have to just keep running their starters out there, and counting on them to round into elevated October form.
That’s what appeared to happen with Yoshinobu Yamamoto on Tuesday night at Great American Ball Park, in what was the right-hander’s most dominant performance of at least the last couple months.
In the Dodgers’ 4-0 win over the Cincinnati Reds, Yamamoto threw a one-hit masterpiece over seven scoreless innings, flashing the kind of ruthless efficiency that defined his heroics during last year’s playoffs.
After walking his first two batters in the first inning, he retired 21 of the 22 after with seven strikeouts and virtually no stress.
“After the first two hitters, it was vintage Yama,” Roberts said. “Just attacking, not trying to be too fine.”
The reigning World Series MVP hadn’t exactly been struggling lately, of course. Just last week, he held the Reds to one run over seven innings with 10 strikeouts back in Los Angeles.
But what Yamamoto did on Tuesday was different, keyed by quick and easy outs on soft and harmless contact.
It’s what he did as the ace of last year’s postseason staff, and what he will need to do again as the Dodgers go for a World Series three-peat this fall.
“I’d like to carry this,” Yamamoto said through an interpreter of his renewed stuff, “into October.”
The Dodgers are hoping they won’t have to ask as much out of Yamamoto this time around; that they need him to pitch back-to-back complete games (like he did in Game 2 of the NLCS and Game 2 of the World Series) or provide back-to-back nights of season-saving heroics (following up a victorious Game 6 start in the Fall Classic with a winning three-inning appearance out of the bullpen in Game 7).
But in a postseason environment, it’s impossible to know what exactly will be required.
“You can’t just try to create that during the regular season because you want these guys as strong and healthy for the October run [as possible],” Roberts said pregame. “But it’s one of those things that, once we get to the postseason, all bets are off and everyone is going to do what they can to contribute.”
It would help, of course, if the Dodgers’ currently Shohei Ohtani-less offense can keep turning a corner, with Tuesday bringing more positive –– albeit subtle –– signs.
The biggest development: Freddie Freeman returned to the lineup amid his ongoing right knee injury, and finally snapped out of a 3-for-30 slump by collecting three singles in the first, fifth and seventh innings.
“Feels better today than he did yesterday,” Roberts said, after Freeman missed his third game in the last week on Monday, “which is a good thing.”
The Dodgers’ scoring, meanwhile, came from elsewhere.

That was all enough to help the team lower its magic number to clinch the National League West to one.
Still, when it comes to October, no position group will be more important than the Dodgers’ rotation.

CINCINNATI –– Every day, Tarik Skubal learns something new about playing for the Dodgers.
Monday's lesson: Clinching a playoff spot warrants only subtle celebrations.
"It's different than anything I've experienced, for sure," Skubal chuckled on Monday night, after the Dodgers recognized their 14th consecutive postseason berth with only a subdued postgame champagne toast and brief speech from manager Dave Roberts.
"But," the club's new star pitcher added, "I think it just speaks to the people in this room and what they expect out of this team. That was cool. A little toast and move on. Forget it happened. We've got more to accomplish this season."
Consider it the latest step in Skubal's acclimation process with the Dodgers –– another little moment that made him feel more at home with his new team.
He's now six weeks on from his emotional trade from the Detroit Tigers at the deadline.
And he's starting to find a comfort level that, after an uneven start to his Dodgers tenure, is helping him look more like the star pitcher he is accustomed to being.
"Constantly learning each other and developing relationships –– a lot of that stuff you don't realize, no one writes about that kind of relationship –– but I think it matters, it matters a lot. I probably underestimated that a little bit," said Skubal, who had spent the entirety of his career in Detroit before his marquee move to the Dodgers.
"But just communicating, having an open dialogue with everyone, all these guys, on what I like to do, what I'm comfortable with and honestly what I'm uncomfortable with … I think we're developing a real good relationship," he added.
And as a result, as manager Dave Roberts noted, "I think the last couple [outings he has made] have been his best."
That was certainly true on Monday, when Skubal spun a gem with the Dodgers' postseason berth in the balance.
He delivered his first scoreless start with the team by blanking the Reds over seven innings at Great American Ball Park. He gave up just three hits and one walk while striking out nine batters in a 90-pitch domination.
"To take the mound on the night that we had a chance to clinch, and we did it," Roberts said, "I think that's something he should be proud of."
More important to Skubal was the way it reflected his growing familiarity with the Dodgers' catchers and pitching department.
He noted he only shook Will Smith off one time all night. He praised the rhythm he has developed with pitching coaches in pre-game prep meetings. And he credited it all with helping him eliminate some perfectionist tendencies that hampered his first month with the team (when he gave up nine runs in 24 innings while lacking the ruthless efficiency that made him a reigning back-to-back Cy Young Award winner).
"I think a lot of the struggles have been 'me vs. me,' thinking too much out there and not competing the way I know how to compete," Skubal said. "Sometimes I try to be too perfect with things instead of just attacking guys over the middle of the plate and letting my stuff play, especially early in games, behind in the count, just not trying to be too fine."
To put it more simply, Skubal added, it was a process of "trying to find the rhythm of who I know I am."
And to people around the team, it's no coincidence that has happened as he's carved out a place in his new clubhouse, as well.
"He's just chill," pitching coach Mark Prior said. "You can joke around with him. You can talk to him."
Few players have grown closer with Skubal than Blake Snell to this point. They've sat side-by-side in the dugout during games, locked in constant conversation. They were pulling practical jokes on one another Tuesday, knocking over each other's chairs in the clubhouse. They've even begun making Step Brothers-inspired jokes about being new best friends on social media.
"I think we're best friends," Snell deadpanned. "Some days, he agrees."
Snell told the California Post that their relationship blossomed naturally, with Snell immediately being struck by how Skubal was "very confident and very secure with who he is" even amid new surroundings.
Two other observations:
"I didn't think he was that funny," Snell joked, describing a side of Skubal that came out Monday night when he razzed backup catcher Hunter Feduccia about a snazzy short-sleeve dress shirt and matching pair of brown slacks ("Outfit of the day!" Skubal declared).
"And," Snell added, "I like how competitive he is. Because it just makes both of us so much better."
That latter dynamic could fuel the Dodgers' entire rotation moving forward, especially entering a postseason in which the group will likely have to carry the team.
"Every time one of our boys go, we want them to dominate, and then the next man up wants to do even better," Snell said. "I think that's very important, to know that we're supporting each other and we're pushing each other to be great, and that we're not focused on just our own achievements. We're focused on our group of starting pitchers all succeeding."
Prior echoed those sentiments, noting that with Skubal specifically: "He wants to have fun. And he wants to win."
Lately, Skubal has been, now on a four-start stretch with only five runs allowed in his last 26 innings.
For the Dodgers, it's a sign of his growth process since being acquired by the club; one that could prove crucial in their three-peat ambitions.
"It's hard to get in that rhythm [and develop] that trust," Roberts said. "But for me, I see just more of the trust in whatever is called, and then you can just go out there [be himself]."

Elly De La Cruz is truly ascending into Tungsten Arm O'Doyle territory of late.
Monday night saw him completely destroy a baseball, one that was conservatively estimated at 457 feet as it buzzed past the power stacks in left-center field in Great American Ball Park en route to exiting the stadium altogether. It was reminiscent of the superblast he hit from the other side of the plate off Los Angeles Dodgers ace Tarik Skubal just a week ago, feats of strength irreplicable by just about any other sole on the planet.
The Cincinnati Reds lost last night, though. Elly's homer was their lone run in a 4-1 loss to those very same Dodgers, a loss that officially eliminated the Reds from any miracle chance at a spot in the postseason. It also sunk them to 10 full games under .500 at 70-80, and this season is rapidly deteriorating into yet another one to forget and chuck onto the scrap-heap of memories of this once proud franchise.
I digress.
Rhett Lowder has a lot to improve upon as he heads into a vital offseason for his overall development. Anything short of a rapid change of form means the Reds need to build in even more redundancy in their starting depth plans for 2027, and there's been precious little in the way of advancement from their former 1st round pick so far in his own disappointing 2026. He'll get the start tonight, while the Dodgers will counter with Yoshinobu Yamamoto.

Dodgers celebran 14to pase seguido a los playoffs con discreto brindis e igualan récord
CINCINNATI — Los Dodgers de Los Ángeles celebraron su 14ta clasificación consecutiva a la postemporada de las Grandes Ligas, para igualar un récord, con un brindis de champán tras la victoria del lunes por la noche por 4-1 sobre los Rojos de Cincinnati.
Las celebraciones más grandes llegarán después.
“Es difícil decir que alguna vez se sienta rutinario, pero esa es la expectativa aquí. Siempre me río cuando aseguramos un lugar en la postemporada: simplemente hacemos un brindis pequeño y agradable”, dijo el tercera base Max Muncy. “Los muchachos que no han estado aquí ven eso y esperan un poco más. Eso pasa cuando aseguras la división”.
Los bicampeones defensores de la Serie Mundial, que se unieron a Milwaukee y Tampa Bay como equipos que ya aseguraron un lugar en los playoffs, redujeron su número mágico a tres para un quinto título consecutivo del Oeste de la Liga Nacional y el 13ro en 14 temporadas.
Los Ángeles igualó la racha de postemporadas de los Bravos de Atlanta de 1991 a 2005. Los Bravos alcanzaron cinco veces a la Serie Mundial durante ese lapso, pero la única vez que se consagraron fue en 1995.
“Por suerte lo estamos haciendo un poco mejor que eso”, dijo Muncy sobre los tres títulos de los Dodgers y sus cinco participaciones en el Clásico de Otoño durante esta racha.
Tarik Skubal —quien lanzó siete entradas sin permitir carreras y concedió apenas tres hits— señaló que la manera en que los Dodgers manejaron el hecho de asegurar un lugar en la postemporada fue definitivamente distinta en comparación con las situaciones de clasificación que vivió las dos temporadas anteriores con Detroit.
“Creo que eso habla de la gente que está en este vestuario y de lo que esperan de este equipo. Eso estuvo genial. Un pequeño brindis y a seguir. Olvidar que pasó. Tenemos más por lograr esta temporada”, expresó.
Dave Roberts, quien cumple su 11ma temporada como mánager, dijo que su mensaje durante el brindis fue que los Dodgers han logrado mucho hasta este punto, pero aún no se han acercado a jugar su mejor béisbol.
“Cada año pasan muchos jugadores por aquí, y los muchachos encuentran la manera de dar un paso al frente, y eso es de lo que probablemente me siento más orgulloso: la consistencia de ganar a largo plazo. Cualquier equipo, cualquier organización puede ganar en un año determinado cuando las cosas se alinean, pero hacerlo todos los años, cuando se espera que lo hagas, dice algo sobre toda la organización”, dijo Roberts.
Los Dodgers (91-59) actualmente son el segundo sembrado en la Liga Nacional. Están dos juegos y medio por delante de Atlanta y están dos juegos detrás de Milwaukee por el primer puesto.
Un pase directo en la primera ronda es importante en cualquier momento, pero especialmente este año para los Dodgers, que no están a plena capacidad. El primera base Freddie Freeman arrastra molestias en la rodilla derecha y Shohei Ohtani, dos veces Jugador Más Valioso de la Liga Nacional, está en la lista de lesionados de 15 días debido a una inflamación en el bíceps derecho.
“Dado cómo están nuestros muchachos en términos de salud, conseguir esa semana sería enorme. Aun así, tenemos que jugar bien para cerrar la temporada y llegar a ese punto”, dijo Roberts antes del juego del lunes.

item.content:encoded:
The two-time reigning World Series champion Los Angeles Dodgers are closing in on the National League West title and still have their sights on the NL’s top seed.
Despite the positives, the Dodgers are limping into the opener of a three-game series against the host Cincinnati Reds on Monday.
Los Angeles (90-59) enters play having dropped two straight against the Miami Marlins, including a 6-4 loss on Sunday that saw the club allow four runs in the ninth and a walk-off homer.
Maybe even more concerning is the injury status of manager Dave Roberts’ star players. After placing Shohei Ohtani on the injured list on Friday with knee and biceps ailments, Roberts announced plans to keep first baseman Freddie Freeman out of the lineup on Monday as he deals with right knee tendinitis.
“(Freddie) is obviously not moving as well as he’s used to,” Roberts said. “I’ll give him a chance to recover and then he’ll be back in there on Tuesday. He’s doing everything he can to prepare, but it’s been obvious the last week that he’s not himself in the box.”
Freeman, 37, sat on Wednesday and Friday before returning to the lineup and going 0-for-8 the last two games. The 10-time All-Star is batting .293 with 16 home runs and 66 RBIs this season.
Tarik Skubal (9-7, 2.84 ERA) will make his eighth start since being traded from Detroit to the Dodgers and his second against the Reds in as many appearances. The 29-year-old tossed 7 1/3 innings of two-run, four-hit ball against Cincinnati on Tuesday. The left-hander struck out five and walked two in a 3-2 win.
Skubal has a 2.93 ERA with the Dodgers and has surrendered two earned runs or fewer in four of his last five starts. Still, the two-time American League Cy Young Award winner believes he has more to give. Coming off the longest outing of his short Los Angeles career, Skubal is beginning to live up to his lofty expectations.
“I think that’s ultimately the job of a starting pitcher,” Skubal said of his longest start with the Dodgers on Tuesday. “One, to give your team a chance to win every time you’re out there, and two, to eat as many innings as you can. … I don’t think I’ve thrown the ball as well as I know I’m capable of yet.”
Skubal is 2-0 with a 1.88 ERA in two career starts against the Reds.
With only a few starts left in what’s been a lackluster year, Nick Lodolo (3-4, 5.12) is hoping to correct an inconsistent personal stretch for the Reds (70-79). The 28-year-old has battled through a pair of stints on the injured list due to a blister on his left index finger.
Since returning on Aug. 11, Lodolo has failed to complete five innings in four of six starts. The left-hander faced Skubal and the Dodgers in a losing effort on Tuesday, when he allowed three runs on five hits across 4 2/3 frames. He struck out six and walked three, extending a seven-start stretch without a win.
“I thought early, he wasn’t commanding the ball,” Reds manager Terry Francona said of Lodolo’s last start. “When he got into the third, fourth and fifth (inning), I actually thought he got better. I really wanted him to get through that fifth. I thought it would have been good for him.”
In three career starts against Los Angeles, Lodolo is 0-2 with a 5.52 ERA.
–Field Level Media

Los Dodgers se aseguran el pase a los playoffs y aspiran a su tercera Serie Mundial consecutiva
El equipo de Los Ángeles se encuentra actualmente en posición de asegurarse uno de los dos primeros puestos de la Liga Nacional junto a los Milwaukee Brewers, que también tienen garantizada una plaza en la postemporada. En la Liga Americana, los Tampa Bay Rays ya se han clasificado.
Los Dodgers de Los Ángeles, que aspiran a su tercer título consecutivo de la Serie Mundial, aseguraron el lunes su plaza en los playoffs tras imponerse por 4-1 a los Reds de Cincinnati. Con un récord de 91-59 y 12 partidos por disputar en la temporada regular, los Dodgers tienen ahora asegurada, como mínimo, una plaza en la serie de comodines.
Los Dodgers se encuentran actualmente en posición de asegurarse uno de los dos primeros puestos de la Liga Nacional —lo que les da derecho a saltarse la primera ronda y a la ventaja de jugar en casa en la serie divisional— junto con los Milwaukee Brewers, que también tienen asegurada su plaza en la postemporada. En la Liga Americana, los Tampa Bay Rays ya se han clasificado.
Los Dodgers, con su generosa inversión, vencieron a los Yankees de Nueva York en la Serie Mundial de 2024 y se impusieron a los Blue Jays de Toronto el año pasado.
Los fichajes de Skubal y Kyle Tucker convierten a los Dodgers en favoritos aún más claros
Tras incorporar al jardinero Kyle Tucker durante la temporada baja y al lanzador Tarik Skubal —ganador en dos ocasiones del Premio Cy Young— el mes pasado, los Dodgers son los favoritos para completar su triplete.
Podrían convertirse en el primer equipo de la Liga Nacional en ganar la Serie Mundial tres años seguidos y el primero desde los Yankees de 1998 a 2000. Pero llegar a los playoffs por decimocuarta temporada consecutiva no ha sido precisamente un camino de rosas.
Una temporada de altibajos
Tras llegar al parón del All-Star con una ventaja de 11,5 partidos sobre Arizona en la división Oeste de la Liga Nacional —con diferencia, el mayor margen de cualquier líder de división—, los Dodgers sufrieron un bajón de forma. La superestrella polivalente Shohei Ohtani ha estado de baja por lesiones, y no se espera que vuelva a lanzar esta temporada; su rendimiento al bate también ha bajado.
Sin embargo, una racha reciente de ocho victorias consecutivas —la mejor de la temporada— ha restablecido la considerable ventaja de los Dodgers al frente de la División Oeste de la Liga Nacional. Sus rivales más cercanos por uno de los dos primeros puestos son los Atlanta Braves de la División Este de la Liga Nacional.
Kyle Tucker y Teoscar Hernández conectaron sendos jonrones en la cómoda victoria de los Dodgers el lunes por la noche en Cincinnati.

Tarik Skubal threw seven scoreless innings and Teoscar Hernandez hit a two-run homer as the visiting Los Angeles Dodgers beat the Cincinnati Reds 4-1 on Monday night to clinch a playoff spot.
Skubal (10-7) allowed three hits — all singles — while striking out nine and walking one for Los Angeles (91-59), which earned a postseason berth for the 14th straight year and pulled within two games of the Milwaukee Brewers for the National League’s best record. Skubal is 2-0 with a 1.73 ERA in his last four starts.
Nick Lodolo (3-5) threw seven innings of four-run, three-hit ball as he struck out four and walked four in his longest outing of the season. The left-hander’s personal winless stretch extended to eight starts in the loss.
Elly De La Cruz connected for his 27th homer of the year in the ninth inning for the Reds’ only run. Cincinnati (70-80) has dropped six of its last seven and its elimination number dropped to one.
Los Angeles struck first in the second inning as Kyle Tucker belted a solo homer — his 15th of the season and his third in his last five games.
Tucker worked a two-out walk in the fourth and scored on Hernandez’s two-run homer that gave the Dodgers a 3-0 edge.
The Reds threatened in the fifth. Juan Brito singled and JJ Bleday walked with one out, but Skubal struck out Ke’Bryan Hayes and Hector Rodriguez to keep Cincinnati off the board.
After Hernandez walked and stole second in the seventh, Enrique Hernandez lined an RBI single to center to make it 4-0.
Luis Mey tossed a perfect eighth in relief of Lodolo.
Alex Vesia entered for Skubal and threw a clean eighth. In the ninth, Evan Phillips struck out pinch hitter Carlos Jorge before allowing De La Cruz’s 457-foot blast to center. Phillips then retired Sal Stewart and Tyler Stephenson to end the game.

El zurdo se mostró imponente frente a Cincinnati, en una de sus mejores aperturas del 2026.
Una joya de pitcheo de Tarik Skubal (10-7) este lunes en el Great American Ball Park, le dio el triunfo a los Dodgers de los Ángeles 4×1 frente a los Rojos de Cincinnati. Triunfo que le permitió a la novena californiana inscribir su nombre en la postemporada 2026 del mejor béisbol del mundo.

El zurdo no le concedió mayores libertades a la toletería de Cincinnati, maniatándolos por completo durante 7.0 capítulos en los que le conectaron sólo tres inatrapables, otorgó un boleto y abanicó a nueve contrarios, dejó su efectividad en 2.70 y su WHIP en 0.95.
Skubal, quien llegó a Los Ángeles desde Detroit en medio de la temporada, completó la que hasta ahora ha sido su mejor apertura desde que se sumó a los líderes del Oeste del Viejo Circuito.
Postemporada 14 al hilo
Tras la victoria frente a los Rojos, los dirigidos por Dave Roberts hicieron oficial su clasificación a la postemporada por vez número 14 de forma consecutiva. En ese lapso sólo perdieron el banderín de su División en una ocasión, fue en la temporada 2021 cuando con récord de 106-56 escoltaron a los Gigantes de San Francisco (107-55).
Ahora el objetivo principal de los Dodgers (91-59) en esta recta final de temporada regular, será arrebatarle el mejor registro de la Liga Nacional a los Cerveceros de Milwaukee, equipo que actualmente juega para 93 triunfos por 57 descalabros.

Dodgers might be forced to leave Edwin Díaz off postseason roster
- Click here to listen to this article
-
- Edwin Díaz struggled in his rehab start Sunday, and Dave Roberts is making it clear the Dodgers “got to see something” from the closer to put him on the playoff roster.
- The Dodgers placed reliever Edgardo Henriquez on the 15-day injured list and recalled Bobby Miller and Paul Gervase.
CINCINNATI — Even as the Dodgers clinched a postseason berth with their 4-1 win over the Reds on Monday, bullpen uncertainty loomed.
When they get to the playoffs, who’s going to take the ball in high-leverage situations?
Their options are dwindling. Edgardo Henriquez landed on the 15-day injured list Monday with low back discomfort, ruling him out for the rest of the regular season. Edwin Díaz was so shaky in his rehab assignment Sunday that a spot on the postseason roster isn’t guaranteed.
“We have to go with our best pitchers, as far as performance, talent, all that stuff,” manager Dave Roberts said before the Dodgers opened a four-game series against the Reds. “So my bet is that he will be [on the roster]. But there’s got to be some kind of evidence or something for us to sort of bet on. And so my bet is, yes, but we’ve still got to see something.”
The Dodgers clinch a playoff berth with their 4-1 victory over the Cincinnati Reds, reaching the postseason for a record-tying 14th consecutive year.
Díaz (neck) had the worst outing of his triple-A rehab assignment, surrendering five runs and issuing two walks in two-thirds of an inning. The dud put his return timeline in doubt. His next rehab appearance is scheduled for Wednesday.
“I think the world of him, the baseball card looks great,” Roberts said. “But where we’re at, there’s got to be something for us to be able to hang our hat on. And he knows that. He knows that. He wants to pitch well. So for me, Wednesday, we’ll be watching closely.”
So, who’s still in play?
Tanner Scott remains Roberts’ go-to in save situations. And Alex Vesia, Evan Phillips, Brock Stewart, Jack Dreyer and Blake Treinen all have experience in late innings.
On Monday, starter Tarik Skubal gave the group a much-needed break with seven shutout innings. He limited the Reds to three hits and a walk, cruising through their lineup almost three times in 90 pitches.
The Dodgers pulled ahead by four runs, on home runs from Kyle Tucker and Teoscar Hernández, who have both broken out of slumps, and an RBI single from Kiké Hernández.
With the game still relatively tight, Vesia entered in the bottom of the eighth to face the left-handed heavy bottom of the order. He retired the side.
Phillips and Treinen both were warming in the ninth when the Dodgers got a runner to second base with one out. When they failed to score him, Phillips jogged in to face the top of the order. He surrendered a high-flying solo homer to Elly De La Cruz on a fastball above the zone but avoided further damage.
Before the game, the Dodgers added two fresh arms to the bullpen. They recalled right-handers Bobby Miller and Paul Gervase, as they put Henriquez on the IL and optioned right-hander Emmet Sheehan.
Henriquez will undergo imaging on the area, which Roberts said stretched to his side near his oblique.
“The hope is we’ll get him back in the postseason,” Roberts said.
Roberts said he didn’t know what the move meant for Sheehan, who in his past two starts limited opponents to one run and recorded 15 strikeouts in a combined 11 ⅔ innings.
“Some of it’s probably contingent on Roki [Sasaki], and we’ve got another start coming up down the road here, as far as a bullpen kind of situation,” Roberts said. “So I don’t know, but Emmet’s done everything he can do in his power to force our hand, which I love. The last two have been really good.”
Sasaki (right middle finger blister) could start Thursday. His bullpen session Monday marked the first time he had tested covering the sensitive area on his finger with Dermabond, Roberts said.
“We just can’t put him in a position to go backward,” Roberts said.
The Dodgers also have more bullpen reinforcements coming.
Another bullpen addition is left-hander Kris Bubic, who met the team in Cincinnati and is in place to make his Dodgers debut later this week. Bubic made his last rehab appearance for triple-A Oklahoma City on Sunday, so Roberts said the Dodgers likely won’t activate him off the 60-day injured list until Wednesday at the earliest.
The Dodgers acquired Bubic from the Kansas City Royals at the trade deadline this year. He’d been on the IL since May, first with a low-grade flexor strain in his left forearm, and then a shoulder impingement setback.
In six triple-A rehab appearances over 5⅔ innings, Bubic didn’t yield a run and he limited opponents to two hits and two walks.
Roberts was noncommittal about Bubic being a high-leverage option.
“Seems like all of our games are leverage these days,” he said.
By not putting Shohei Ohtani on the injured list in July or in August, the Dodgers may have compromised the two-way star’s ability to be healthy for the playoffs.

item.content:encoded:
CINCINNATI – On a night when they were nearly blanked for a Major League-leading 17th time, the Reds were once again reminded of what a playoff team looks like across the field in the other dugout.
The only thing standing between the Reds and another goose egg was a monumental home run from Elly De La Cruz with one out in the ninth. The 98 mph fastball from Evan Phillips was actually above the strike zone. De La Cruz crushed it a Statcast-projected 457 feet, the third-longest home run of his career and the longest by a Red this season.
“Maybe I'll pick it up on the way home,” joked Reds manager Terry Francona. “That's pretty impressive. It’d be a lot more fun to talk about if it put us ahead … but it was still impressive.”
The homer, De La Cruz’s 27th, soared into the alley between the bleachers in right-center and the right tall stack as fans looked into the back of the stands to get a glimpse of the ball actually landing. It also extended De La Cruz’s season-long on-base streak to 21 games, the longest active streak in MLB and the second-longest of his career.
But for highlights, that was it for the Reds.
The real frustration of this season was encapsulated by starter Nick Lodolo coming out after six innings, allowing four runs on just three hits. He went over to the ball bag and slammed his right hand into it twice out of anger.
The reason?
Free passes. Lodolo walked four and struck out four while allowing four runs on just three hits in seven innings.
“I think [two of the] walks I had scored,” Lodolo said. “Obviously not every walk you have is going to score every night, but it's something that this year that has killed me. I was just frustrated with it.”
“Oh, I don't care. I don't,” Francona said of Lodolo's reaction. “I care what they do on the mound. I don't care about hitting the ball bag.
“Three hits, but you know, two of them left the ballpark, [and one] after a walk. But still ... it's a dangerous team over there. We got behind the wrong guy.”
Lodolo (3-5) made two mistakes on the night. A 1-0 fastball left up to Kyle Tucker, who crushed it down the right-field line for a 1-0 Dodgers lead in the second. His second mistake -- a first-pitch 91.6 mph fastball that Teoscar Hernández lifted just over the fence in right-center for a two-run roundtripper and a 3-0 Dodgers lead in the fourth, after a walk to Tucker.
That was more than enough for Tarik Skubal (10-7), the big addition that the Dodgers traded for at the Deadline. He blanked the Reds on three hits, striking out nine and walking one in seven innings.
“Obviously, one of the best pitchers in the league, if not the best,” Lodolo said. “So you know that going into the game. But regardless who's on the other side, I'm more worried about doing my job and letting our guys handle that. My job is to keep us in the game, give us a chance to win. ... When a guy's rolling like that, you're trying to match it.”
Before the tape-measure blast from De La Cruz in the ninth, the Reds had one threat all night. In the fifth, they had Juan Brito at third and JJ Bleday at second with two outs. But Skubal fanned Héctor Rodríguez to keep Cincinnati off the scoreboard.
Frustration has been a common theme in the past week, as the Reds have dropped six of their past seven games, including four to the Dodgers.
Ironically, the win by the Dodgers Monday night at Great American Ball Park clinched their 14th straight playoff appearance. In those 14 years, the Reds have qualified for the playoffs just three times, including last year, when the Dodgers started their run to a second straight World Series title with a two-game sweep of the Reds in the NL Wild Card round.

The Los Angeles Dodgers placed right-hander Edgardo Henriquez on the 15-day injured list Monday with low back discomfort, ending his 2026 regular season. Los Angeles recalled Bobby Miller from Triple-A Oklahoma City as the corresponding roster move.
Henriquez had developed into a regular bullpen option during his first full major league season, making 61 appearances. MLB.com's Sonja Chen took to X, formerly Twitter, shortly after the club announced the transaction and noted the calendar implications of Henriquez's IL placement.
"Henriquez going on the 15-day IL ends his regular season."
Watch sports LIVE with fuboTV (free trial)
Henriquez last pitched Sunday vs. the Miami Marlins, allowing two earned runs on three hits and one walk over two-thirds of an inning. He also recorded one strikeout and received credit for a hold in Los Angeles' 6-4 loss.
The 24-year-old right-hander finishes the regular season with a 4-1 record and 2.85 ERA across 61 games, including one start. The right-hander struck out 71 and walked 25 over 60 innings while posting a 1.03 WHIP. His 61 appearances ranked 24th in the National League.
The timing of the move prevents Henriquez from returning before the regular season concludes September 27. A 15-day placement Monday makes him eligible to return September 29, when the Wild Card Series begins. The move does not automatically rule him out for the postseason if he recovers and earns a roster spot.
The Dodgers have not announced an MRI result, structural diagnosis, or surgery related to Henriquez's back discomfort. His absence removes another pitcher from a Dodgers staff already dealing with multiple injuries, including Shohei Ohtani's right biceps inflammation.
Miller joins the active roster as Los Angeles continues its four-game road series against the Cincinnati Reds. Henriquez's regular season is over, but the Dodgers could still have the right-hander available for the postseason depending on his recovery.

Los Angeles Dodgers pitcher Roki Sasaki took an encouraging step Monday in his recovery from a right middle-finger blister, throwing a bullpen session ahead of the club's four-game road series against the Cincinnati Reds beginning Monday. The development keeps the 24-year-old in consideration for a return Thursday vs. the Reds, though the Dodgers have not committed to activating him. The Los Angeles Times' Maddie Lee took to X, formerly Twitter, on Monday afternoon with manager Dave Roberts' latest update.
"Roki Sasaki threw a bullpen today and tested out covering the blister wirh dermabond, Dave Roberts said. He's a possibility for Thursday, but 'we just can't put him in a position to go backwards,' so still TBD."
The right-hander has been on the 15-day injured list since August 27 after the blister opened during his start against the Atlanta Braves one day earlier. He lasted 3 1/3 innings and threw 66 pitches before leaving the game.

Monday's bullpen allowed Sasaki to test Dermabond over the healing blister while throwing. The Dodgers remain cautious because another setback could further delay his return as the regular season enters its final weeks.
Sasaki is 5-5 with a 4.60 ERA and 117 strikeouts across 119 1/3 innings and 23 starts this season. His results had improved before the injury, as he posted a 3.05 ERA over 38 1/3 innings in seven starts following the All-Star break.
Thursday remains a possible return date rather than a confirmed activation. The Dodgers have an open rotation spot for the series finale against Cincinnati, but Sasaki's availability will depend on how his finger responds following Monday's bullpen session.
The Dogers head into Monday at 90-59 and atop the NL West as it prepares for the postseason. Getting Sasaki healthy would provide another rotation option, but Roberts' update makes clear that the club will not risk reversing his progress simply to fill Thursday's opening.

Shohei Ohtani se ha perdido seis de los últimos siete partidos de Los Angeles Dodgers debido a las lesiones que ha venido arrastrando esta temporada. La primera fue en la rodilla, una molestia que lo alejó del montículo desde principios de julio y que, con poco tiempo para recuperarse antes de los playoffs, hace casi un hecho que no vuelva a lanzar en 2026. Una baja sensible para los Dodgers en el tramo más importante de la campaña, en el que buscan conquistar su tercera Serie Mundial consecutiva.
Shohei Ohtani to be placed on the injured list (left knee, right biceps), Dodgers manager Dave Roberts announces. pic.twitter.com/AG3VlX3TVe
— MLB (@MLB) September 10, 2026
La segunda lesión que sufrió esta temporada fue en el bíceps, una molestia que ha ido empeorando con el paso de las semanas. Ohtani comenzó a sufrir molestias en el cuello como consecuencia de este problema, lo que obligó a los Dodgers a colocarlo en la lista de lesionados y provocó que se perdiera los últimos encuentros. La buena noticia es que el japonés ha estado trabajando para regresar en este cierre de temporada regular y volver a ocupar su puesto como bateador designado de cara a los playoffs de la MLB.
Ohtani será fundamental en las aspiraciones de los Dodgers
Previo al inicio de la serie ante los Reds en Cincinnati, el mánager de los Dodgers, Dave Roberts, confirmó que Ohtani tiene programado realizar swings desde un tee antes del partido del martes. La actividad representa un paso adelante en su recuperación y mantiene abierta la posibilidad de que pueda regresar a tiempo para ayudar a Los Angeles en los playoffs.
"I think it's important that he does pitch because he has the ability to do it. He's elite."@spillygoat19 shares his thoughts on whether or not he would discourage Shohei Ohtani from pitching in the future.
MLB Network + @NewBalance pic.twitter.com/KqBg6i0pMd
Por fortuna, los Dodgers se prepararon durante la temporada ante una eventual ausencia prolongada de su superestrella. Por esa razón, adquirieron al pitcher Tarik Skubal antes de la fecha límite de intercambios para fortalecer una rotación de lanzadores que buscará llegar en las mejores condiciones a la postemporada.
Shohei Ohtani could resume swinging Monday or Tuesday as he continues recovering from lingering right biceps and left knee issues.
Ohtani is eligible to return from the IL on September 23, giving him a short window to prepare for the postseason.#Dodgers #BlueDynasty pic.twitter.com/l2vdNja7kE
Además, los Dodgers llamó a uno de los mejores prospectos de las Grandes Ligas, Josue De Paula, para aportar a la ofensiva mientras Ohtani se recupera. El pelotero impresionó en sus primeros partidos ante los Marlins, una actuación que le permite a los Dodgers darle mayor tiempo de recuperación a Ohtani con la esperanza de que esté listo para disputar el Clásico de Otoño.

The Los Angeles Dodgers are one win away from clinching a National League playoff berth.
Monday, September 14, the Dodgers begin a three-game series against the Cincinnati Reds for the second time seven games.
Ahead of tonight’s game, the Dodgers make a couple changes in their lineup, one of them involving utility player Tommy Edman.
Tommy Edman is Back in the Lineup vs. the Reds After a Rest Day on Sunday
Per Los Angeles Dodgers reporter David Vassegh, the team announced their starting lineup against the Cincinnati Reds on Monday.
#Dodgers Lineup vs #Reds LHP, Nick Lodolo: Edman CF, Betts SS, Smith C, Tucker RF, T. Hernandez LF, Rojas 2B, Muncy 3B, E. Hernandez 1B, JDP DH, Tarik Skubal SP,” Vassegh wrote on X.
Edman sat out in Sunday’s loss against the Miami Marlins because Dodgers manager Dave Roberts, did not want him playing all three games on a turf field.
“#Dodgers Dave Roberts originally said Josue De Paula would DH all 3 games in Miami,” Dodgers insider Bill Plunket wrote on X ahead of Sunday’s game. “Thought it thru and decided he didn’t want Teoscar Hernandez or Tommy Edman to play all 3 games on turf here. So De Paula gets the start in LF.”
Edman and the Dodgers have been carefully monitoring the center fielder’s ankle, after spending nearly half the season on the injured list. The 31-year-old underwent an offseason ankle surgery and did not return to the Dodgers lineup until June 17.
While the Dodgers primary center fielder Andy Pages, remains on the injured list, Edman has spent most of starts in center.
Despite slashing .257/.339/.390 in 72 games, Edman’s seven game stretch shows signs of a quite the slump.
He’s batting .091 with five strikeouts, two hits, and two RBIs in his last 22 at-bats. Both of hits coming against the Washington Nationals on September 6.
Hopefully yesterday’s much needed rest day gets Edman back where he needs to be.
Los Angeles Dodgers Magic Number to Win NL West is Four
There only 15 days until the first MLB postseason game, and 13 games left in the season for the Dodgers. They can clinch a postseason berth tonight with a win against the Reds.
“LAD can clinch a postseason berth today with a win at Cincinnati *or* losses by both the Padres (@ COL) AND the Diamondbacks (v. MIA),” Dodgers beat writer Katie Woo wrote on X.
For the National League West, the Dodgers’ magic number is four.
After their series concludes against the Reds, the Dodgers are strictly facing NL West opponents. Two series at-home against the San Francisco Giants and San Diego Padres, and rounding off the season on the road to face San Francisco for the final time in 2026.
